clinicalPearls: Caused by truncating variants in KAT6B (MYST4/MORF), a histone acetyltransferase closely related to KAT6A, with the position of the variant within the gene shaping whether the genitopatellar or SBBYSS phenotype results
The defining combination is absent or hypoplastic patellae, external genital anomalies and flexion contractures of the hips and knees
Genital findings include cryptorchidism and scrotal hypoplasia in boys and clitoromegaly in girls
Renal anomalies, particularly cystic or hydronephrotic kidneys, are frequent and require imaging
Microcephaly, agenesis or hypoplasia of the corpus callosum and intellectual disability are typical of the neurological phenotype
Compared with the allelic Say-Barber-Biesecker-Young-Simpson syndrome, genitopatellar syndrome lacks the prominent blepharophimosis and mask-like face but shares patellar involvement
Diagnosis rests on molecular confirmation of a KAT6B variant, with careful correlation of variant location and clinical features
reference.pathophysiology: KAT6B encodes a MYST-family lysine acetyltransferase that acetylates histone H3, promoting a chromatin environment permissive for transcription of developmental target genes. Truncating variants clustered in particular regions of the gene are thought to generate proteins that disturb this acetylation-dependent gene regulation in a manner specific to the genitopatellar presentation, in contrast to variants elsewhere that produce the SBBYSS phenotype. The consequent misregulation of developmental programmes affects patterning of the limbs and patellae, the genitourinary tract and the brain, giving rise to the characteristic skeletal, genital, renal and neurological features.
additionalDifferentials: Other syndromic causes of patellar aplasia with genital anomalies
additionalInvestigations: Exome or genome sequencing to identify KAT6B variants with attention to variant location
Renal ultrasound to detect cystic kidneys and hydronephrosis
Knee imaging to confirm absent or hypoplastic patellae
Brain MRI to assess the corpus callosum and other structural anomalies
Endocrine and genital assessment including evaluation for cryptorchidism
redFlags: Significant renal impairment from cystic or obstructive kidney disease
Airway or feeding compromise in the neonatal period
reference.prognosis: Outlook is determined largely by the severity of renal and central nervous system involvement; intellectual disability is common and often moderate to severe, and orthopaedic and urological problems typically require long-term multidisciplinary management, while renal disease can be the principal threat to health.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish genitopatellar syndrome from the allelic SBBYSS phenotype, which alters counselling and expectations
Overlooking renal cysts or obstruction that can progress to impairment
Attributing patellar aplasia to nail-patella syndrome without genetic testing
Missing corpus callosum anomalies that inform the neurological prognosis
references: GeneReviews — KAT6B-Related Disorders (Genitopatellar Syndrome and SBBYSS)
Nature Reviews — histone acetyltransferases in development and disease
management: No disease-specific therapy exists, so management is supportive and coordinated across multiple specialties
Renal ultrasound surveillance and urological management of cystic and hydronephrotic kidneys, which can be the principal threat to survival
Orthopaedic and physiotherapy management of absent or hypoplastic patellae and of hip and knee flexion contractures
Assessment and surgical management of genital anomalies, including orchidopexy for cryptorchidism, with endocrine input
Neurodevelopmental support for intellectual disability, with brain MRI to define corpus callosum and other structural anomalies
Echocardiographic assessment for associated cardiac defects, and feeding and respiratory support in infancy
Genetic counselling for the KAT6B disorder, which usually arises as a de novo variant
